newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn parliament committee to approve 1997 budget.
newsitem.headline: Bonn parliament committee to approve 1997 budget.

text.p: The German parliament's lower house budget committee met on Thursday to put the final touches on its budget for 1997, the key year for deciding the starting line-up of countries participating in European monetary union.

Faced with falling tax revenues, Finance Minister Theo Waigel has fought a bruising personal battle to slash federal spending and hold the 1997 deficit to 56.5 billion marks ($37.52 billion), comfortably below the threshold three percent of economic output set out in the Maastricht Treaty.
The budget debate has at times nearly split Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition government, and Kohl himself threatened to quit in heated closed-door sessions.

Coalition officials made the last major alterations to the 440 billion mark budget in an emergency meeting late on Sunday, when they agreed an additional three billion marks in spending cuts that brought the debate back on keel.
They also agreed to increase unemployment outlays by 6.4 billion marks in the face of record unemployment.
The parliamentary committee may agree some further spending cuts but was not expected to make major changes on Thursday. The closed meeting was expected to last until late evening.
The 1997 budget will then have its second and third readings in the full parliament in two weeks.

The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) called several cabinet ministers to speak before the committee on Thursday, starting with chancellery minister Friedrich Bohl and agriculture minister Jochen Borchert.
It was unclear whether Waigel would address the meeting.
SPD budget spokesman Karl Diller said before the meeting the government needs to find 10 billion marks in spending cuts, not three billion.

The most controversial spending cuts agreed earlier this week were a billion marks trimmed from the Federal Labour Office, despite unemployment soaring above 10 percent, its highest level since World War Two.

Coalition leaders also cut 200 million marks from the defence budget, but critical decisions on cutting a tax raised to pay for east German reconstruction and on procuring the Eurofighter combat jet now have been put back to December.

Most German aerospace jobs are in Waigel's home state of Bavaria, and opposition politicians have accused him of protecting jobs in his own patch against potentially deeper spending cuts. ($1=1.5059 Mark)
